title: Tamar (2 Samuel 13)
hookLine: a king's daughter is violated and silenced; the text names the wrong plainly

lines: A PLAN TO GET HER ALONE.
cards: A note before we begin: today's story is about sexual violence. It's told without detail, and if you need to stop, that's fine. Tamar is a daughter of King David, the sister of Absalom.
Her half-brother Amnon becomes fixated on her. His cousin and friend Jonadab hands him a plan: pretend to be sick, and ask the king to send Tamar to cook for you. David sends her.
She kneads the dough in front of her brother and bakes the cakes. She has no reason to be afraid.

teach.b: Amnon sends everyone out and takes hold of her. The first thing to notice: Tamar speaks. She says no.

This is not done in Israel, she says; do not do this wanton thing. She asks where she could carry her shame, and what he would become. She even offers a way out: speak to the king; he will not keep me from you.
He will not listen. He is stronger, and he forces her.

teach.h: HE FORCES HER, THEN HATES HER.
teach.b: Then, the text says, he hates her more than he had loved her, and has her thrown out and the door bolted. Tamar doesn't go quietly.

teach.h: SHE TEARS HER ROBE AND CRIES ALOUD.
teach.b: She tears the long robe the king's unmarried daughters wore, puts ashes on her head, lays her hand on it, and goes away crying aloud. The second thing to notice: the Bible names this as a wrong.
It doesn't blur it or blame her. It gives her words, and records her grief in public. Then the silencing.
Absalom says: hold your peace, my sister; he is your brother; don't take this to heart. And Tamar "remained desolate" in her brother Absalom's house. King David hears all of it and is very angry.
The text doesn't say he does anything. Absalom says nothing to Amnon, good or bad, and waits. Much of what follows grows out of that silence: a murder, a rebellion, a war between father and son.
Why is this chapter here? In a palace where the powerful wanted it quiet, the text remembers her name, her words, and her torn robe.

how: Jews read the story of Tamar as part of the book of Samuel; some teachers today use it to talk openly about sexual violence and about believing those who come forward.

o: David's daughter, who said no and was silenced
a palace cook who served at the king's table
Absalom's wife, who warned him about Amnon

p: very angry, but the text records no act

s: she spoke, refused, offered a way out, and went away crying aloud.
it names what Amnon did as a wrong and records her grief in public.
Absalom told her to hold her peace
he said, he is your brother; don't take this to heart. she remained desolate in his house.

games.q: you're Absalom. your sister comes to you with her robe torn and ashes on her head. what do you say?
o: I believe you, and I'll stand with you.
let's go to the king together.
games.why: Absalom tells her to hold her peace and not take it to heart. she remains desolate, and the family's silence shapes everything that follows.

practice: Think of someone who might one day bring you something painful, and picture yourself listening without what Absalom said: not hush, not don't take it to heart, just I believe you, and I'm here.
If this story touched your own life, simply breathe, and know that yours deserves to be told too. If you pray, you can remember Tamar and everyone like her.

wordCard.voice: Tamar. A king's daughter who said no, was wronged, and was told to be quiet, and whose story the text refused to drop. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Tamar, the name as written in 2 Samuel 13.

carryVoice: Your line: her story is told. The text refused to let it be hushed. Until tomorrow, gently.
